headline: SB police officer beaten to death in Savar after protesting assault on auto-rickshaw driver
summary: A Special Branch sub-inspector was fatally assaulted in Savar after intervening in an attack on an elderly auto-rickshaw driver. His son was also critically injured and their garment factory was vandalized during the incident.
details: A sub-inspector of the Special Branch (SB) of police, Md Altaf Hossain, 57, was beaten to death in Savar yesterday evening. The incident occurred after he allegedly protested when a group of youths assaulted an elderly auto-rickshaw driver.

Altaf's son, Md Arif, was also seriously injured in the attack, and a small garment factory owned by the police officer was vandalized. The incident took place around 10:00 PM in the Janata Housing area of Aminbazar.
Altaf, posted with the Dhaka Metropolitan Police, lived in a rented house in the area with his family. He also ran the garment factory on his own land with his son.

According to family members and eyewitnesses, Altaf was returning home when he saw several youths in a private car assaulting an elderly auto-rickshaw driver near his residence. When he protested, the youths allegedly turned on him.

Altaf identified himself as a police officer and sought refuge in his factory. However, the youths reportedly called 15-20 others, attacked the factory, vandalized machinery, and beat Altaf and Arif, leaving them unconscious before fleeing.
Neighbors rushed Altaf and Arif to Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital. Doctors there declared Altaf dead, while Arif is currently undergoing treatment in critical condition.
Savar Model Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Saiful Alam confirmed the incident, stating that police have visited the scene and are working to identify and arrest those involved.

headline: Dengue infections highest in 3 years with 110 deaths; experts warn of uncontrolled spread
summary: Bangladesh faces its worst Dengue outbreak in three years, with over 40,000 patients hospitalized and 110 deaths by early September. Infections are spreading rapidly beyond Dhaka, overwhelming hospital capacity.
details: Bangladesh has recorded its highest Dengue infection rate in three years between January and August, indicating significant gaps in government preparedness and mosquito control initiatives. Experts warn that infections could spiral out of control in September.

The alarming aspect is that Dengue is now spreading at the same pace in cities and rural areas beyond Dhaka and Chittagong, including Khulna, Rajshahi, and Barisal. This widespread transmission puts immense pressure on an already strained healthcare system, which is also dealing with ongoing measles infections and deaths.

Since July, Dengue infections have been on the rise, with a sharp increase in hospital admissions in August. By the first week of September, government hospitals are full, and private hospital beds designated for Dengue patients are also rapidly filling up.

According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), over 40,000 Dengue patients were hospitalized by September 4 this year, the highest in three years for the same period. A total of 110 patients have died from Dengue so far this year.

While over 16,000 patients are from the Dhaka division, the significant number of cases outside Dhaka is a major concern. This highlights that mosquito control efforts remain primarily Dhaka-centric, and Dengue treatment facilities outside the capital are largely inadequate.

Research by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) indicates that the Den-3 strain of the Dengue virus is dominant this year, with Den-2 also circulating significantly. Entomologists and public health experts had previously warned that the warmer weather and intermittent rain could lead to a severe outbreak in August-September.

Despite directives from the highest policy-making levels, no science-based plan or initiative for Aedes mosquito eradication has been observed. Mosquito control activities have largely relied on traditional spraying, rather than involving the public in destroying breeding grounds and larvae.

A harsh reality is the near absence of mosquito control activities outside Dhaka, Chittagong, and a few other major cities. The failure to develop scientific and effective strategies for Aedes mosquito control over two and a half decades is considered a major state failure.

Citizens are paying the price for this failure with their valuable lives. In this period of high inflation, the cost of Dengue treatment has become a significant burden for many families, with some forced to take loans to cover medical expenses.

Despite claims of preparedness from the Health Directorate, the sight of relatives rushing patients from one hospital to another in search of beds indicates insufficient capacity. It is crucial to increase Dengue treatment opportunities and government support at both public and private levels.

The government must recognize that Dengue cannot be controlled solely through patient identification and treatment preparation. Immediate, realistic, and effective measures involving the public are needed to control the Aedes mosquito, which carries the Dengue virus.
